lessons.title: The Concept and Duties of a Welfare State
lessons.notes_html:
What a Welfare State Means

A welfare state is a state which looks after the basic needs of its citizens and makes them able to live a life of peace and calm. The objectives of such a state are ending ignorance and illiteracy, poverty and destitution, and injustice from society. The citizens are given such opportunities and environment in which all citizens can develop their natural abilities and get opportunities. In a welfare state the basic needs of the citizens are fulfilled and their welfare is the first responsibility of the state.

Duties of a Welfare State

  • Protection of the life, property and honour of the citizens.
  • Protection of the basic rights of the citizens and giving them justice.
  • Giving facilities of education, health, employment and housing.
  • Helping the poor, orphans, widows and the disabled.
  • Protecting the borders of the country and maintaining law and order.
  • Fair distribution of resources, and making plans for the welfare of the citizens and implementing them.

Concept of an Islamic Welfare State

  • In Islam supreme authority lies with Allah Almighty and the state protects the life, property and honour of its citizens.
  • There is justice for all people without discrimination and all are equal in the eyes of the law.
  • The ruler is bound by the basic symbols and commands of Islam and fears Allah.
  • The rulers are servants of the people and always think about the welfare of the people.
  • The rulers live the lifestyle of an ordinary person and are answerable to the people.
  • The concept of an Islamic welfare state is that it should establish equality.

Role of the Individual in a Welfare State

  • Every person should remain loyal to the state and be ready to sacrifice when needed.
  • Every citizen should respect the rights of fellow citizens and protect their life, property and honour.
  • The individual should not misuse public utilities, such as electricity, gas, water, public parks and transport.
  • A citizen should take part in welfare activities individually or collectively, and keep the environment clean.
  • All citizens should pay taxes regularly and obey the law of the country.
  • Every citizen should get education and make better use of national resources.

Key Points

  • The government is trying that in Pakistan an equal and just society is established.
  • In Islam supreme authority lies with Allah Almighty.

lessons.title: National Goals, Self-Reliance and a Just Society
lessons.notes_html:
National Objectives of Pakistan

  • Establishment of an Islamic society: Establishing an Islamic society according to Islamic teachings and the principles of democracy.
  • Struggle against exploitation: Struggle to end poverty, ignorance and illiteracy.
  • Protection of the state: Keeping the country safe from internal and external dangers.
  • Self-sufficiency: Becoming self-sufficient economically.
  • Unity and peaceful coexistence: Unity and solidarity with Muslim countries, and promotion of international peace through peaceful coexistence.
  • Welfare state: Struggle for the establishment of a welfare state.

Need for Self-Sufficiency in Food

Food is a basic need of the people and without proper food the health of the people deteriorates. If the health of the people is not good, their performance will decrease and it will affect the progress of the country. Shortage of food increases inflation. The majority of Pakistan's population is connected with agriculture and a large part of the national income comes from agriculture. Through self-sufficiency in food the country becomes free from external pressure and national honour increases.

Need for Peace in the Whole World

  • The present world has become a global village — because of science and technology nations have come closer to one another.
  • The problems of one country affect other countries, and without peace progress and prosperity are not possible.
  • Wars cause great loss of human lives, property and resources.
  • Pakistan is a peace-loving country and it supports the efforts of the United Nations. Islam also teaches peace, tolerance and brotherhood.

Government Steps for Mass Education

  • Reforms in the education sector (E.S.R.) — introducing a system which fulfils the ideals and needs of Pakistan.
  • Including Pakistan Studies and Islamiat in the curriculum, and discouraging the trend of commercialisation in education.
  • Improving the service conditions of teachers.
  • A programme of giving scholarships to intelligent and poor students under Pakistan Bait-ul-Mal.
  • Starting a literacy campaign on radio and TV, the "Education for All" programme — free books and facilities in non-formal educational institutions — and establishment of the Education Foundation.

A Just and Equal Society

A just and equal society is a society in which all individuals get equal rights and equal opportunities. In such a society no person remains deprived of his rights, everyone gets facilities of education, health and employment, the law is equal for all and everyone can get justice, and people have freedom of expression and liberty. There is a spirit of love, brotherhood and cooperation and society becomes strong. The government of Pakistan is trying its best to make its society equal and just, but financial and economic problems are a big obstacle in it.

Continuous Constructive Effort

Awareness of national objectives is maintained only through continuous effort. The nation has to be taught the value of hard work — the dignity of labour — the standard of education has to be raised, people have to be led on the path of progress through guidance and encouragement, and welfare programmes have to be advanced. Since 1947 the different sectors of Pakistan's economy have progressed a lot, but the need of the time is that Pakistan should be made a welfare state as soon as possible.

Key Points

  • The majority population of Pakistan is connected with agriculture.
  • Pakistan is self-sufficient in the production of wheat and rice (cotton, sugar and fertiliser are also included).
  • Economic progress leads towards prosperity.

lessons.title: Rights and Duties of a Citizen and Corruption
lessons.notes_html:
Rights of a Citizen

Every citizen has some basic rights. Personal liberty: Every person has the right to freedom in his action and thought, provided it does not harm others. Freedom of expression and religion: Every citizen has freedom to express his opinion and follow his religion. Education and health: Education is a basic need and every citizen should get the facility of education and health. The citizen also has the right to protection and equality of the law.

Duties of a Citizen

  • Regard for the rights of others: Not violating others' rights while using one's own rights.
  • Obedience to the law and loyalty to the country.
  • Giving priority to national interests over personal interests.
  • Being ready for the defence of the country.

Duties as a Student

  • The first duty is to get education and complete our education.
  • To take part in national services, such as blood donation and civil defence, at election time or during holidays.
  • To maintain discipline in educational institutions.
  • To collect aid for disaster victims and help them.
  • To respect teachers and parents and obey the rules of the school.

Corruption — Meaning and Effects

Corruption means the misuse of powers for personal benefit by violating the law — such as taking bribes, cheating in examinations, and nepotism. Its effects on society are that the government does not get the money needed for building schools, hospitals and roads, roads become a cause of more accidents, and people have to pay higher prices for things. Students pass examinations by cheating, which destroys their ability, lawlessness increases, and society suffers moral and social harm. The government has set up institutions like the National Accountability Bureau (NAB), the Federal Investigation Agency (FIA) and the Anti-Corruption Department to fight corruption.

Key Points

  • In democracy there is freedom of opinion.
  • Ordinary citizens elect their representatives through their votes.
  • National interests should be given priority over personal interests.

Activities

Practical work: Make a chart of the rights of a citizen — write the rights: personal liberty, freedom of expression, freedom of religion, right to education, right to health, equal protection of the law, right to vote, right to property, right to employment, and write a short meaning of each right in front of it.

Practical work: Complete the table about corruption. Types: Bribery, nepotism, cheating in examinations, misuse of government funds. Causes: Greed, weak enforcement of the law, absence of punishment, lack of moral training. Effects: Obstacle in development works, inflation, lawlessness, moral ruin. Measures for prevention: Institutions like NAB, FIA and the Anti-Corruption Department, strict punishments, transparency. What you can do: Neither give nor take bribes, do not cheat, raise your voice against corruption, obey the law.

lessons.title: Human Rights and the UN Universal Declaration 1948
lessons.notes_html:
Basic Characteristics of Human Rights

Human rights are the rights which are present by inheritance in every person because of being a human being. Human rights come with the birth of a human being — they are natural. They are equal for all human beings, without any distinction of race, colour, sex, religion or nationality, and they cannot be taken away from anyone. They protect the honour and dignity of human beings.

  • Human rights include life, liberty, security and equality.
  • Education, health, freedom of expression and freedom of religion are also included in human rights.

The UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights 1948

The General Assembly of the United Nations adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (UDHR) on 10 December 1948, which has 30 articles. The purpose of the Declaration is to maintain peace in the world and the welfare of human beings.

Important Provisions of the Declaration

SubjectRight
Basic rightsRight to equality, life, liberty and security
FreedomsFreedom from slavery and torture, freedom of movement
Legal rightsEquality before the law, right to a fair trial
Civic rightsRight to asylum, right to nationality and marriage, right to property
Expression and participationFreedom of belief and expression, right to assembly and participation in government
Social rightsSocial security, work, rest, adequate standard of living and participation in cultural life
Education — Article 26Emphasis is laid on the right to education in Article 26

Key Points

  • Human rights are the rights which are present by inheritance in every person because of being a human being.
  • The General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights on 10 December 1948.
  • In Article 26 of the United Nations Human Rights Declaration, emphasis is laid on the right to education.

lessons.title: Human Rights in Pakistan — Condition and Protection
lessons.notes_html:
Rights of Citizens under the 1973 Constitution

Under the Constitution of 1973, the citizens of Pakistan have equality and equal protection of the law, freedom of expression and assembly, freedom of religion, right to education, right to property, right to employment and security.

Duties of Citizens

  • Obedience to the law and respect for the rights of others.
  • Correct use of the vote and defence of the country.
  • Giving priority to national interests and paying taxes.
  • Protecting public property.

Rights and duties are linked with each other — the use of rights is possible only through fulfilling duties.

Classification of Rights and Duties

RightsDuties
Equality of all citizens in the eyes of the lawObeying the law
Freedom of expressionUsing the vote in elections
Liberty and securityRespecting difference of opinion
Protection of propertyCleanliness of the neighbourhood and defence of the country

Using the vote is both a right and a duty, but in the book's activity it is listed as a civic duty.

State of Human Rights in Pakistan

The Constitution of Pakistan guarantees the rights of all citizens without any distinction, and Pakistan is responsible for upholding international human rights standards, but in practice there are still challenges. Because of lack of literacy, poverty, corruption and weak enforcement of the law, violations of rights take place.

Suggestions for Protection

  • Increase public awareness about human rights, and spread education.
  • Strengthen institutions like the Ministry of Human Rights, the Human Rights Cell (HRC) of the Supreme Court and the Ombudsman.
  • Strict enforcement of the law and quick investigation of violations.
  • Special protection of the rights of women, children and the disabled.

Activities

Research: Investigate a case of violation of human rights and set up a research on the role of the state in protecting the rights of citizens. Select the news of one recent case of violation of human rights, from a newspaper, TV or the internet, investigate its facts, the right of the affected person and the action taken on it, and write a short research including the guarantee of the Constitution, the Ministry of Human Rights, the HRC of the Supreme Court and the role of the Ombudsman.

Group activity: Discuss in groups the rights of citizens under the 1973 Constitution and the rights given to citizens under the 1948 Declaration. Divide into two groups — one group prepares a model speech on the rights of citizens under the 1973 Constitution and the other group on the rights given under the 1948 Universal Declaration, and present them in class. The purpose of the discussion is to understand the similarities and differences between the two — the Constitution is the country's legal guarantee and the Declaration is international principles.

lessons.title: The Ombudsman and Rights-Protection Institutions
lessons.notes_html:
The Ombudsman — Court of the Poor

The institution of the Ombudsman is generally considered the "court of the poor". The Ombudsman is a government official appointed by the government or the parliament and attends to administrative complaints. The aim of the Ombudsman is to end administrative injustice and give quick justice to the citizens.

  • Any affected person can lodge his complaint through post, fax, e-mail or the Ombudsman's website.
  • The Ombudsman receives the complaint, starts investigation on it and gives instructions to the concerned institution.
  • In Pakistan the Ombudsman hears and investigates citizens' complaints against administrative injustice of government institutions, and promotes transparency and accountability in administrative matters.
  • The Ombudsman has powers like a civil court — he can summon witnesses, demand documents and punish contempt of his decision. With a few changes, he has the same powers as a High Court.

Institutions and Their Duties

InstitutionDuties / Role
OmbudsmanHearing and investigating administrative complaints, instructions to concerned institutions, quick justice, and promotion of transparency and accountability
Human Rights Cell (HRC) of the Supreme CourtAction on applications about violations of human rights, quick and free relief to the public, receiving applications through post and correspondence on them, calling for reports on complaints, immediate justice administratively, and action on complaints of Pakistanis living abroad

Ways of Harassment

  • Harassment at the workplace: Harassing women at the workplace.
  • Verbal harassment: Harassing through abuses, threats and insulting talk, which injures a person's honour and whose legal prevention is necessary.
  • Physical harassment: Beating or causing physical pain.
  • Psychological harassment: Frightening, causing fear and putting pressure.

The Parliament of Pakistan passed the Protection Against Harassment of Women at the Workplace Act in 2010, whose aim is to give women a safe environment at the workplace.

Key Points

  • The institution of the Ombudsman is generally understood like a court of the poor.
  • The Ombudsman has, with a few changes, the same powers as a High Court, such as the power to punish contempt of his decision.
  • The Parliament of Pakistan passed the Act for protection against harassment of women at employment and workplaces in 2010.

Activities

Mock court: Set up a mock court in class — one student becomes the judge, some become lawyers and some become witnesses. Select the news of a recent case of violation of human rights, investigate its facts, hear the statements of witnesses and decide which right was violated and what its remedy should be. The purpose is to understand the process of justice practically.

Group discussion: Divide into groups and criticise and discuss the duties and powers of the Ombudsman, and present it before the class — one group argues for the benefits of the Ombudsman, such as quick and cheap justice and the court of the poor, and the other group argues on its limits, such as some matters being outside its powers, like matters of courts and the armed forces. Then each group presents its conclusions before the class.

mcqs.why: The correct answer is the 'court of the poor'. The lesson states that the institution of the Ombudsman is generally considered the court of the poor, because it gives quick justice to citizens against administrative injustice.

mcqs.q: The Ombudsman is a government official appointed by:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is the government or the parliament. The lesson defines the Ombudsman as a government official appointed by the government or the parliament who attends to administrative complaints.

mcqs.q: The aim of the Ombudsman is:
options: To end administrative injustice and give quick justice to the citizens
To make laws for the country
mcqs.why: The correct answer is to end administrative injustice and give quick justice to the citizens. The lesson adds that the Ombudsman receives the complaint, starts investigation on it and gives instructions to the concerned institution.

mcqs.q: A complaint can be lodged with the Ombudsman through:
options: Only by appearing in a court
Post, fax, e-mail or the Ombudsman's website
mcqs.why: The correct answer is post, fax, e-mail or the Ombudsman's website. The lesson states that any affected person can lodge his complaint through any of these means.

mcqs.q: The Ombudsman has powers like a civil court — he can:
options: Summon witnesses, demand documents and punish contempt of his decision
mcqs.why: The correct answer is summon witnesses, demand documents and punish contempt of his decision. The lesson states that the Ombudsman has powers like a civil court and, with a few changes, the same powers as a High Court.

mcqs.q: With a few changes, the Ombudsman has the same powers as:
mcqs.why: The correct answer is a High Court. The lesson's key points state that the Ombudsman has, with a few changes, the same powers as a High Court, such as the power to punish contempt of his decision.

options: Matters of the courts and the armed forces
